claims.claim: Step-based computer tutoring (one step, one hint at a time) is about as effective as one-to-one human tutoring, so a well-structured AI tutor can substitute for much of the parent's teaching time without a large loss.
claims.source_title: The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems
claims.key_numbers: Human tutoring d = 0.79 vs no tutoring; intelligent (step-based) tutoring d = 0.76; earlier beliefs of d = 2.0 for human tutors and d = 1.0 for ITS were not supported. The search summary's figure for answer-based/substep tutoring was ambiguous and is not relied on.
claims.implication: The maths-tutor-session rules 'never give the answer first' and 'one hint at a time' are exactly the step-level interaction that produced the 0.76 effect; keep them and copy them into a Spanish tutor skill, which currently does not exist (Spanish has only the app and the platform-building skill).

claims.claim: Gains from tutoring systems look much larger on the system's own tests than on standardised tests, so in-session exit tickets will overstate exam readiness.
claims.source_title: Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Meta-Analytic Review
claims.key_numbers: 50 controlled evaluations; median effect 0.66 SD (50th to 75th percentile); improvement depended 'to a great extent' on whether it was measured on locally developed or standardised tests (the size of the gap is not shown in search summary).
claims.implication: Treat the tracker's 'secure' (80% unaided in-session) and exit-ticket scores as provisional; only timed AQA past papers marked with the real scheme should drive the Dec 2026 Foundation mock (>= grade 5) and the Feb 2027 tier decision before entries close ~21 Feb 2027. The dashboard should show latest full-paper grade beside coverage %, not coverage alone.

claims.claim: Across 107 comparisons, intelligent tutoring systems raise test scores by a moderate amount (about 0.4 SD), so an AI tutor supplements but does not replace the hours needed to teach the 24 untouched maths topics and 98 untouched Spanish topics.
claims.source_title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
claims.key_numbers: 107 effect sizes; 14,321 participants; average improvement 0.43 SD in test scores.
claims.implication: Plan the timetable around coverage arithmetic (topics remaining divided by weeks to the May/June 2027 exams) rather than expecting the tutor to compress learning; the tracker should show 'topics per week needed' next to the countdown badge so the parent can see whether the pace is realistic.

claims.claim: Unguarded ChatGPT-style help raises practice scores but lowers performance once the AI is taken away, whereas a tutor with guardrails (hints, no direct answers) removes most of that harm.
claims.source_title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
claims.authors_year: Bastani, Bastani, Sungu, Ge, Kabakcı & Mariman, 2025 (PNAS)
claims.key_numbers: Field experiment with nearly 1,000 high-school maths students; practice grades +48% with 'GPT Base' and +127% with 'GPT Tutor'; students with unguarded access 'perform worse on their own' afterwards; harm 'largely mitigated' by GPT Tutor safeguards. The exact size of the unassisted-exam decrement is not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: The 'never give the answer first' rule is load-bearing and must also apply to the Spanish app's AI Chat and to any quick-help (shape B) use. Because students used the bot as a crutch, the tracker should log hints-per-question and whether the exit ticket was done unassisted; an exit ticket answered with Claude's help should not count towards 'secure'.

claims.claim: A purpose-built LLM tutor with expert-written scaffolds, step-by-step reasoning and anti-hallucination guardrails beat a well-run active-learning class on learning gains, time and engagement.
claims.source_title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
claims.authors_year: Kestin, Miller, Klales et al., 2025 (Scientific Reports)
claims.key_numbers: 194 Harvard undergraduates, Fall 2023, crossover by week; AI-tutored students learned 'more than twice as much' as the active-learning class, in less time, with higher self-reported engagement and motivation. Effect size in SD units not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: The winning design had lesson content authored by experts and fed to the model, not generated on the fly; the maths skill should carry per-topic worked-example and misconception notes (e.g. the recurring A4 sign and collecting-terms errors) so Claude teaches from vetted material, and the Spanish side needs the same before a tutor skill is written. Note the sample is adults at an elite university, not 13-year-olds.

claims.claim: Across 35 experimental studies, ChatGPT-style tools have a moderate positive effect on learning outcomes, so the expected gain is real but modest and depends on how the tool is used.
claims.source_title: ChatGPT's impact on student learning outcomes: a meta-analysis of 35 experimental studies
claims.authors_year: authors not shown in search summary, 2026 (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications)
claims.key_numbers: 35 studies published 2022-2024; 4,193 participants; 'moderately positive effect' on cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes. Pooled effect size not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: The parent should judge the system by the student's own unassisted paper scores over time (the tracker's attempts list), not by the presence of AI tutoring; a moderate average effect leaves plenty of room for this particular set-up to under- or over-perform.

claims.claim: Students working with ChatGPT improved their immediate task scores but showed 'metacognitive laziness', offloading the thinking that produces durable knowledge.
claims.source_title: University students offload critical thinking, other hard work to AI
claims.authors_year: Fan et al., 2024 (British Journal of Educational Technology, 'Beware of metacognitive laziness'), reported by The Hechinger Report, 2025
claims.key_numbers: 117 students; laboratory experiment (reading, essay writing and revision in English); the 'potential metacognitive laziness' finding refers to dependence on AI and offloading thought. Whether allocation was randomised is not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: The logged behaviours (answers without working, all parts answered when one asked, arithmetic in prose) are offloading signatures; the skill should require working to be typed before any hint is given and end each taught topic with a one-minute 'explain it back without notes' step, logged as a per-item outcome.

claims.claim: Reviews of AI tools in STEM classrooms find over-reliance and over-trust that can disrupt students' ability to plan and monitor their own problem-solving.
claims.source_title: Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric-Systematic Review Approach (2005-2025)
claims.authors_year: authors not shown in search summary, 2025
claims.key_numbers: Bibliometric and systematic review covering 2005-2025; counts and effect sizes not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: Add a cheap calibration step: before each exit ticket the student predicts her score, and the tracker stores predicted vs actual; a persistent gap is the earliest sign that AI-assisted practice is creating an illusion of mastery. This is a planning/monitoring support that fits the parent's no-gamification stance.

claims.claim: In adults with ADHD, immediate (0 s) feedback impaired probabilistic learning relative to controls, while a short delay (3-6 s) brought performance level with controls; 'faster feedback is always better for ADHD' is not safe to assume.
claims.source_title: Feedback Timing Modulates Probabilistic Learning in Adults with ADHD
claims.authors_year: authors not shown in search summary, 2018 (Scientific Reports)
claims.key_numbers: Adults with ADHD vs controls; feedback at 0 s, 3 s or 6 s after each choice; ADHD performance comparable to controls with delayed feedback, diminished with immediate feedback. Sample size not shown in search summary. Laboratory cue-outcome task, not academic content; no children.
claims.implication: Keep instant right/wrong feedback in the timed Spanish Shooting Gallery (it is a drill she enjoys), but in maths sessions have Claude ask her to re-read her own working for a few seconds and say what she notices before it marks the step; the evidence is thin and lab-based, so treat this as a hypothesis to test against her blank-rate and retry data rather than a rule.

claims.claim: The widely repeated advice that children with ADHD need more immediate, frequent and specific reinforcement than peers (usually credited to Luman et al., 2005) could not be confirmed here because the search budget ran out before that search executed; it is a belief without a retrieved source.
claims.authors_year: Luman, Oosterlaan & Sergeant, 2005 (cited from memory, not verified)
claims.implication: Until the ADHD-education research agent confirms this, the system should not rebuild feedback timing around it; the safe default is short practice sets (3-5 items, which the tracker already logs) with feedback after each item, and a note in every skill that the student has ADHD, which no skill currently mentions.

claims.claim: W3C's cognitive-accessibility guidance (a Working Group Note supplementing WCAG) sets out objectives and design patterns for helping users focus, avoiding distraction, making each step clear and not relying on memory.
claims.source_title: Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities
claims.authors_year: W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (COGA), 2021 Working Group Note (year from prior knowledge; the search summary confirms the document, its scope and that it is supplemental to WCAG)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary; the specific pattern names (e.g. help users focus, avoid too much content, make each step clear) were not visible in the search result and are quoted from prior knowledge of the document.
claims.implication: The dashboard is parent-facing, so apply COGA to the student's surfaces: give the Spanish app and any future 'today' view one task per screen, a visible 'step 2 of 4' progress marker, the current instruction kept on screen (so she is not asked to remember 'only the blues'), and a written next-step at the end of every Claude turn.

claims.claim: CAST's UDL Guidelines 3.0 recommend supporting executive function with guides and checklists for goal-setting and by scaffolding lower-level skills so they consume less executive capacity.
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (framework, no effect sizes); the executive-function row covers emotional capacity, building knowledge and strategy development.
claims.implication: Open every maths session with a three-line checklist Claude writes and the student ticks (goal for today, what 'done' looks like, when the exit ticket happens), and close by checking it; the tracker's log_session could store 'goal met / not met / ran out of time', which would also fill the current gap that nothing records how a session ended (e.g. Q4 and Q5 left unsubmitted on 2 Sep).

claims.claim: Practitioner guidance for ADHD users converges on minimal clutter, single-task screens, chunked content, progressive disclosure one step at a time and always-visible progress indicators; this is expert consensus, not trial evidence.
claims.source_title: Designing for Children with ADHD: The Search for Guidelines for Non-Experts - User Experience
claims.authors_year: UXPA Magazine, year not shown in search summary
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary; the same points recur across the practitioner sources returned (Accessibly, Din Studio, Welcoming Web, Medium).
claims.implication: In the Spanish app, show one set and one mode at a time and hide the vocabulary-set picker during a run; in Claude sessions, present one question with one part at a time rather than multi-part questions, which directly targets the 'answers every part when one was asked' habit. A visible session timer is often recommended in these sources but no trial evidence for it was retrieved.

claims.claim: The APA's 2025 health advisory says adolescents are less likely to question the accuracy of AI responses and recommends human oversight, age-appropriate design and limits on AI as a substitute for human relationships; general-purpose chatbots (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) are not designed for mental-health support.
claims.source_title: Health advisory: Artificial intelligence and adolescent well-being
claims.key_numbers: Advisory recommendations only; the '76% of teens concerned about data collection' figure appeared in a secondary source (Newport Healthcare) and is not attributed to the APA advisory here.
claims.implication: Keep Claude's role academic: the maths skill's 'if frustrated pause and suggest a break' rule should hand off to the parent rather than have Claude counsel, sessions should stay reviewable by the parent (the log_session summaries already enable this), and the student should be told plainly that Claude can be wrong and that a hint disagreeing with the mark scheme is settled by the mark scheme.

caveats: The session's web-search budget was exhausted after the first 12 searches; a planned second batch (Bastani's exact unassisted-exam decrement, Kestin's effect size, Luman et al. 2005 on reinforcement in ADHD, Socratic-hint-vs-answer trials, COGA pattern names, a peer-reviewed systematic review of ADHD interface design, visual-timer trials, UK DfE generative-AI guidance, the 'AI makes you smarter but none the wiser' study, Tutor CoPilot results, and the Fan et al. 2024 BJET paper directly) did not run. Claims touching those topics are marked accordingly.

Only C9 is ADHD-direct, and it studied adults on a laboratory probabilistic-learning task, not children learning school content. Every tutoring-effectiveness finding (C1-C8) is general-population, and C5 is Harvard undergraduates. No study of AI tutoring with ADHD adolescents was found.

No trial evidence was retrieved for the specific guardrail of 'withholding answers' in isolation; Bastani et al.'s GPT Tutor bundled hints, guidance and answer-withholding, so the effect cannot be attributed to answer-withholding alone.

No RCT of ChatGPT or Claude tutoring with secondary-school students in maths or languages was found in 2025-2026 results; the closest are Bastani (high-school maths, Turkey), a quasi-experimental high-school programming study (153 students, Interactive Learning Environments, 2025) and several medical/dental-student RCTs.

Metcalfe, Kornell & Finn (2009, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19933453/) found delayed feedback beat immediate feedback for Grade 6 vocabulary learning in typical children; it was dropped to stay within 14 claims but supports adding an end-of-run review of missed items in the Spanish app.

Tutor CoPilot (Wang et al., 2024, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.03017) appeared in results but its numbers were not shown; it is relevant as a model of AI assisting a human tutor (the parent) and was omitted for the same reason.

The ADHD interface guidance (C13) comes from practitioner articles and blogs; the COGA and UDL documents (C11, C12) are expert-consensus guidelines that cover cognitive and learning disabilities broadly, not ADHD specifically.

Not verified by search but worth the parent checking: consumer AI chat services commonly require users to be 18 or older, so a 13-year-old should be using Claude through the parent's supervised account and the skills, not an account of her own.

The 'immediate corrective feedback in ADHD' question is unresolved here: C9 points one way (a short delay helped adults with ADHD), the unverified conventional advice (C10) points the other, and the child-vocabulary evidence (Metcalfe 2009) favours delay in typical children. The ADHD-education agent should settle it before the skills are rewritten.
